question: A 57-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of crampy abdominal pain and foul-smelling, watery diarrhea. One week ago, she underwent treatment of cellulitis with clindamycin. She has developed shortness of breath and urticaria after treatment with vancomycin in the past. Her temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Her leukocyte count is 12,800/mm3. An enzyme immunoassay is positive for glutamate dehydrogenase antigen and toxins A and B. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient's condition?

options.opa: Inhibition of cell wall peptidoglycan formation
options.opb: Blocking of protein synthesis at 50S ribosomal subunit
options.opc: Inhibition of bacterial topoisomerases II and IV
options.opd: Generation of toxic free radical metabolites
options.ope: Inhibition of RNA polymerase sigma subunit

analysis: The patient is presenting with symptoms of Clostridium difficile infection, which is confirmed by the positive enzyme immunoassay for glutamate dehydrogenase antigen and toxins A and B. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this condition is typically metronidazole or vancomycin, both of which work by blocking protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit in bacteria.
